facts.text: The name Diwali, or Deepavali, comes from Sanskrit words for lamp and row, so it means a row of lights.
Diwali lasts five days and follows the Hindu lunar calendar; its main day falls on a new moon, usually in October or November.
In northern India the festival recalls Prince Rama's return to Ayodhya after 14 years of exile; people are said to have welcomed him with lamps.
Families clean and decorate their homes to welcome Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth, and many Indian businesses treat Diwali as the start of a new financial year.
Sikhs mark the release of Guru Hargobind on the same days, and Jains mark the day Mahavira reached nirvana.
Diyas are small clay oil lamps; families line them up outside their homes, and they stand for the victory of light over darkness.
People decorate floors and doorsteps with rangoli, colorful patterns made from colored powder, rice flour, sand or flower petals.
On the fourth day, families exchange gifts and sweets with loved ones; traditional sweets include gulab jamun and jalebi.
Al Biruni, an 11th-century Persian scholar, recorded Hindus celebrating Diwali on the new-moon day of the month Kartika with oil lamps on temples and rooftops.
More than a billion people around the world take part in Diwali.
Potters in Kumbharwada, a potters' district of Mumbai, say they make about half of their yearly sales in the month before Diwali.
In 2016 a local clay diya cost about 50 US cents, while cheaper plastic lamps imported from abroad cost about a quarter.
Diwali fireworks add to air pollution, and New Delhi has banned firecrackers in recent years.
On 19 October 2025, Ayodhya lit 2,617,215 diyas along 56 riverside ghats, setting a Guinness World Record.
Deepavali was added to UNESCO's list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity at a meeting held in New Delhi from 8 to 13 December 2025; it is India's 16th entry.
The Mumbai potters said they had no unsold lamps, and one seller said that customers who want genuine clay lamps keep coming to them.
